clips.text_en_b1: Stuck with a condo at 27. In 2021 at 22 I made random crypto money from Dogecoin. Lived two years with no job, perma vacation, dropped out of school, bought a condo for $230K. Money ran out. Went back, graduated, now make $100K and live in my condo. I have student debt and credit card debt.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon regrets early crypto gains, stuck with condo and debt

signal.rationale: Post is a lifestyle regret story, not an active DOGE trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: Stuck with a condo at 27. In 2021, at 22, I struck it lucky on Dogecoin, quit my job, dropped out of school, and blew two years living the dream before dropping $230K on a condo. Once the money dried up, I knuckled down, finished my degree, and now earn around $100K while sitting on the property. Between student loans and credit card debt, I'm essentially back where I started, watching my peers quietly overtake me.
clips.text_en_c1: Another cautionary tale of Dogecoin windfalls squandered within a single cycle. At twenty-two, a speculative punt on the meme coin yielded enough to fund two years of leisure: no employment, perpetual travel, and a hasty withdrawal from university. He purchased a condominium for $230,000, assuming the gravy train would never end. It did. By twenty-seven, the capital had evaporated, forcing a return to the workforce, a belated graduation, and a $100,000 salary that barely services the residual credit card and student debt. He laments having tasted unearned affluence only to resume the ordinary grind of consume, repay, repeat.
clips.text_en_c2: At 27, I find myself shackled to a condominium purchased during the most gilded episode of an otherwise improvised life. In 2021, aged 22, I made a conspicuously random fortune from Dogecoin, abandoned my studies, and spent two years in what became an involuntary, open-ended holiday. With tuition abandoned and every conventional constraint suddenly negotiable, I bought a $230,000 condo as though permanence could be underwritten by market luck. The money inevitably evaporated, after which I returned to work, completed my degree, and began earning $100,000 a year. I still inhabit the condo, but the carefree existence it symbolised has been replaced by student loans, credit-card debt, and the bitter familiarity of work, consumption, and repetition. I resent having sampled a rich man’s lifestyle, only to discover that the bill arrived with compound interest.

clips.text_en_b1: Why buy BTC after the pump? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Why does everyone always want to buy after the move already happened? This is the same pattern every cycle on /biz/.

signal.rationale: OP warns against FOMO buying post-pump; no clean long or short setup, weak bearish lean on retail flow

clips.text_en_b2: Why on earth do people pile into BTC after the pump? The chart goes absolutely nowhere for weeks, so nobody touches it. Then it rips 15% in a day, and suddenly every retail trader on /biz/ wants in. Buying the breakout after it's already happened is financial suicide, yet this same dysfunctional pattern repeats itself every single cycle. You'd think people would eventually learn.
clips.text_en_c1: Bitcoin consolidates for weeks on end and retail shrugs it off entirely, dismissing the asset as dead money. Then it rips fifteen percent in a single move, and suddenly every latecomer scrambles for exposure at the worst possible juncture. This reflexive behaviour, buying only after the rally has already printed, is a textbook recipe for portfolio annihilation, and it recurs with monotonous regularity across every cycle on /biz/. Anyone who has lived through a prior bull run recognises the pattern: those who arrive at the party after the music has stopped invariably end up holding bags.
clips.text_en_c2: The sheer predictability of the exercise is almost more demoralising than the losses it produces. Bitcoin spends weeks oscillating within a range narrow enough to render attention itself redundant, yet scarcely has the market settled into torpor than a 15% surge arrives and everyone suddenly develops an urgent appetite for exposure. Capital that treated stagnation as conclusive evidence of irrelevance now pursues the instrument at precisely the moment when the most conspicuous move has already occurred. Such behaviour is less an investment thesis than voluntary participation in a liquidity transfer, rather like buying front-row tickets after the performance has become the talk of the town. On /biz/, this ritual recurs with metronomic regularity: impatience during consolidation, euphoria after expansion, and inevitable bafflement when prices retrace.

clips.text_en_b2: OpenAI dropped a video on September 8th claiming their Astra model, powered by GPT-6, had cracked a problem after burning through roughly $20 million in compute. Trouble is, researcher Tristan Buckmaster pointed out the framework looked suspiciously similar to his own pipeline, which he had been building for months using OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude. If the labs are essentially cannibalising independent researchers, what's even the point anymore.
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI unveiled Astra on September 8th, a GPT-6-powered system purportedly resolving a long-standing problem at a compute cost approaching twenty million dollars. Almost immediately, researcher Tristan Buckmaster observed that the underlying methodology bore an uncanny resemblance to work he had independently assembled using OpenAI's own Codex alongside Anthropic's Claude. If frontier labs are now absorbing methodologies devised by individual researchers who lack comparable resources, the entire incentive structure for independent inquiry collapses. The optics here are indefensible, and the accompanying video lays out what amounts to a flagrant ethical conflict of interest.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI announced on September 8 that Astra, a model built with GPT-6, had solved a problem after an estimated $20 million had been devoted to computation. The claim projected an atmosphere of laboratory triumph, until researcher Tristan Buckmaster observed that the underlying approach bore an uncomfortably close resemblance to work he had himself been developing with OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. If systems capable of ingesting, synthesising, and operationalising published research can also absorb the unpublished labour from which future discoveries emerge, the old argument for mastering a field begins to look almost quaint. Expertise has not become less valuable, but its returns are being privatised elsewhere.

clips.text_en_b1: New OECD PISA study of 760,000 students across 91 countries shows global math and reading scores are cratering. Kids are getting dumber everywhere except China. Chinese students are the smartest by a huge margin. The elite Level 5 in maths starts at 607, and the average Chinese kid scores 612. Normal Chinese kids are at a level considered elite elsewhere.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread on China dominating OECD PISA scores
clips.text_en_b2: Fresh OECD PISA data covering 760,000 students across 91 countries paints a brutal picture: global maths and reading scores are in freefall, and kids worldwide seem to be getting dumber. China is the glaring exception, storming in the opposite direction while everyone else declines. The elite Level 5 maths threshold sits at 607, yet the average Chinese student already hits 612, meaning a normal kid there outperforms so-called elites abroad.
clips.text_en_c1: The latest OECD PISA assessment, encompassing 760,000 students across ninety-one participating nations, confirms a global regression in both mathematical literacy and reading comprehension that should alarm any policymaker paying attention. Worldwide averages are cratering, yet Chinese students have bucked the trend decisively, posting gains that leave every Western competitor in their wake. The threshold for elite Level 5 performance in mathematics sits at 607, and the average Chinese pupil now scores 612, a figure that places ordinary mainland students at what Western systems would classify as exceptional. STEM-oriented pedagogy appears vindicated once again.
clips.text_en_c2: A new OECD PISA assessment, drawing upon roughly 760,000 students across 91 countries, records a brutal deterioration in global mathematics and reading performance. Everywhere else, the prevailing interpretation is that children are becoming demonstrably less capable, although the numbers suggest that complacency and deteriorating educational systems may be doing at least as much damage as any alleged decline in innate ability. China moves decisively against the international tide, leaving its competitors with little room for flattering comparisons. In mathematics, elite proficiency begins at Level 5 with a score of 607, while the average Chinese pupil reaches 612—an ordinary national result that would be regarded as exceptional among many of the country’s foreign counterparts. The broader lesson is difficult to evade: where STEM is treated as the central educational imperative, competence follows.

clips.text_en_c1: Blizzard employees have ratified what can fairly be described as a landmark union contract, one whose provisions may well establish a new industry-wide benchmark for game developers. The timing is particularly pointed: while management has been aggressively pursuing AI integration throughout the production pipeline, the workforce has organised and pushed back with remarkable cohesion. Companies that lean on artificial intelligence to paper over deteriorating labour relations will eventually find themselves outmanoeuvred by organised, mobilised staff.
clips.text_en_c2: Blizzard employees have secured a historic union contract that may establish a consequential benchmark for game developers throughout the industry. The timing is especially significant because, while workers are celebrating an unusually tangible labour victory, the company is pressing aggressively to embed artificial intelligence in production. The contrast is almost too neat to be accidental: technological futurism at the corporate level, concrete protections for those who must live with its consequences. Staff have not merely resisted automation rhetorically; they have negotiated safeguards governing how AI may be used in the workplace. That distinction matters in an industry where “innovation” is often invoked to convert anxiety, insecurity, and expendability into something resembling managerial policy.

clips.text_zh: 4chan fit友鬧CICO dogma係tautology，同問點解Elon咁有錢答「因為佢使少過賺」一樣廢。講到尾點解肥先係重點。CFD輸錢同肚腩都係同一個病。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Is there anything more retarded than the calories in calories out dogma? If you are getting fatter, sure you are storing more calories. But CICO never tells you WHY it happens. It is like asking why Elon Musk is rich and answering because he took in more money than he spent. That explains nothing. Why is this low IQ shit still repeated everywhere?
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread roasting CICO as a tautology
clips.text_en_b2: Is there anything more brain-dead than the calories in, calories out dogma? Sure, getting heavier means you're storing more energy, fine. But CICO never bothers explaining why that's happening in the first place. It's basically like asking why Elon Musk is rich and answering "because he earns more than he spends." Technically correct, utterly useless. Yet somehow this lazy tautology keeps getting parroted everywhere as if it were profound insight.
clips.text_en_c1: The calories-in-calories-out dogma remains the most insufferable tautology in fitness discourse, and it explains precisely nothing of substance. Granted, anyone accumulating adipose tissue is necessarily storing surplus energy, but the framework offers no causal mechanism whatsoever. It is functionally equivalent to attributing Elon Musk's fortune to the observation that his income exceeds his expenditure, a statement that is technically accurate yet utterly devoid of explanatory power. The hormonal, behavioural, and metabolic drivers of weight gain are entirely elided by this reductive formulation, yet the lowest-common-denominator fitness crowd continues parroting it as gospel.
clips.text_en_c2: The calories-in, calories-out doctrine has attained the rare distinction of being repeated so often that repetition has begun to masquerade as explanation. Of course, someone who is growing fatter is retaining more energy than they expend; caloric arithmetic describes the destination, not the route by which the body reached it. Asking why Elon Musk is rich and receiving “because he earns more than he spends” as an answer would reproduce precisely this category error. The statement may be arithmetically compatible with wealth, but it leaves appetite, enterprise, inheritance, timing, and risk almost entirely unexamined. Fat accumulation likewise raises the questions that CICO contrives to evade: why is hunger being triggered, why has expenditure fallen, why are metabolic signals behaving abnormally, and why does one person remain lean while another stores energy with apparently effortless efficiency?…

clips.text_en_c1: Ishiguro has taken it upon himself to rank his own manga creations, illustrating select characters in swimwear for added whimsy, while fielding tangential anecdotes about his formative years. Notably absent from the rankings is Kon-senpai herself, though her super-deformed counterpart from an adjacent gag series makes an appearance. clips.text_en_c2: Tonight’s /a/ content is an exercise in unapologetic wholesomeness: Ishiguro ranks his favourite characters from his own manga, renders them in swimsuits, and then wanders cheerfully through the sort of miscellaneous anecdotes that polished promotional material usually discards. Kon-senpai is conspicuously absent, yet her super-deformed incarnation from the associated gag manga makes a welcome compensatory appearance, preserving the ritual of inclusion through aesthetic absurdity. The revelation that Ebi-chan was inspired by Ishiguro’s first elementary-school crush lends the character an added tenderness; fiction is shown to have preserved, rather than merely invented, an early ideal of affection. There is something quietly restorative about watching an artist discuss his creations with evident intimacy, as though distance from the work has made gratitude more persuasive than critical detachment.
